paragraphs.text: You who are weaned from milk, you who are drawn away from the breast, welcome affliction upon affliction, welcome hope upon hope, yet a little while, yet a little while, through contempt of lips, through another tongue.

You too, then, most God-fearing Ambrose and most pious Protoctetus, are, in Isaiah's words, no longer fleshly or infants in Christ. You have advanced in your spiritual stature and no longer need milk but solid food. So hear, as those weaned from milk and drawn away from the breast, how athletes who have been weaned are promised in prophecy not a single affliction but affliction upon affliction. Whoever does not thrust away the affliction upon affliction, but welcomes it like a noble athlete, at once welcomes also hope upon hope, which he will enjoy not long after the affliction upon affliction. That is what "yet a little while, yet a little while" means.

And even if those who are strangers to the language of the holy Scriptures despise and belittle us, calling us either impious or fools, let us remember that the hope upon hope, which is to be given to us in yet a little while, will be given "through contempt of lips, through another tongue." Who would not welcome affliction upon affliction in order to welcome at once also hope upon hope? He would reckon with Paul that "the sufferings of the present time", with which we, as it were, purchase blessedness, "are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed" to us from God. All the more so since "our momentary light affliction" is light in fact as well as in name for those who are not weighed down by their surroundings. The more it abounds, the greater and more abundant "the weight of eternal glory" it "works for us". This holds if, at the time when men afflict us and wish, as it were, to crush our souls, we turn our ruling faculty away from our hardships and look not at the present hardships but at what God's grace has laid up for those who, because of their endurance in these things, have contended lawfully in Christ. For God multiplies his benefits and, beyond the worth of the contestant's labors, gives as much as befits God to give, who does not haggle, who is generous, and who knowingly magnifies his own graces toward those who, as far as they could, have shown by despising the earthen vessel that they love him with their whole soul.

I think that God is loved with the whole soul by those who, out of great eagerness for communion with God, draw the soul away and separate it not only from the earthly body but from every body. For them, laying aside "the body of humiliation" happens without any distraction or dragging back, when the moment allows them, through what is reckoned death, to strip off "the body of death" and to be heard when they pray in the apostle's words: "Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" For who among those "groaning in this tent" because they are weighed down by the corruptible body will not first say, "Who will deliver me from the body of this death?" and then also give thanks? He sees that, once he has been delivered from the body of death through this communion, he will cry out in holiness: "Thanks be to God through Christ Jesus our Lord." If anyone finds this hard, he has not "thirsted for God, the mighty, the living", nor "longed for God as the deer longs for the springs of water", nor said, "When shall I come and appear before the face of God?" Nor has he reasoned within himself as the prophet reasoned. When it was said to the prophet, "Where is your God?", he "poured out his soul within him" every day. He rebuked his soul when, through weakness, it still grew downcast and troubled, and said: "For I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, as far as the house of God, with the voice of rejoicing and thanksgiving, the sound of those keeping festival."

I would pray, then, that throughout the whole present contest you remember the great reward laid up in heaven for those who are persecuted and reviled for righteousness' sake and for the sake of the Son of Man, and that you rejoice, exult and leap for joy, as the apostles once rejoiced that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for his name. If you ever feel your soul shrinking back, and it tries, as far as it can, to throw into confusion even the mind of Christ that is in us, let that mind say to it: "Why are you downcast, O soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I shall give thanks to him," and so on. Would that the soul were never troubled at all! Even before the tribunals themselves, and with bare swords brought down on the neck, may it be guarded by "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding," and be calm, reckoning that those who are away from the body are at home with the Lord of all himself. But if we are not great enough always to keep our tranquility, at least let the soul's trouble not pour out or show itself to those outside. Then we will have room to make our defense before God, saying to him: "O my God, my soul is troubled within me." The word also urges us to remember what is said in Isaiah: "Do not fear the reproach of men, and do not be overcome by their contempt." God is plainly present over the motion of heaven and of the things in it. He also governs what his divine art brings about on land and sea in the birth, structure, nourishment and growth of every kind of animal and plant. It is absurd, then, to shut our eyes and not look to God, and instead to turn our eyes in fear toward those who will soon die and be handed over to the punishment they deserve.

God once said to Abraham, "Go out from your land." To us, perhaps, it will soon be said, "Go out from the whole earth." It is good to obey this, so that he may quickly show us the heavens, in which is what is called the kingdom of heaven. One can see that life is full of contests over many virtues, and one can see those who contend in them. Many others among those who belong to God's portion will be thought to have contended for temperance. Some have died with courage, keeping their resolve for the sake of the common Master. Those skilled in examining arguments have cultivated prudence, and those resolved to live justly have devoted themselves to justice. Against each virtue there wages war either the mind of the flesh or many of the things outside us. But for piety only the chosen race contends: "the royal priesthood, the holy nation, the people for God's own possession." The rest of mankind do not show, even in appearance, that when there are forces opposed to the pious they are resolved to die for piety, preferring death with piety to life with impiety. Each of those who wish to belong to the chosen race is persuaded to listen to God speaking at every moment. This holds even when he is the target of plots by those who claim to have many gods but are in fact godless. God says: "You shall have no other gods besides me," and, "You shall not remember the name of other gods in your hearts, nor shall it be named by your mouth." Therefore such people believe God with the heart unto righteousness and confess him with the mouth unto salvation. They understand that they will not be justified unless they believe God with their heart so disposed. Nor will they be in salvation unless their word matches their inner disposition. For they deceive themselves who think that, for reaching the goal in Christ, "for with the heart one believes unto righteousness" is enough, even if "and with the mouth one confesses unto salvation" is missing. One may even say that it is better to honor God with the lips while keeping the heart far from him than to honor him with the heart while the mouth does not confess unto salvation.

He says, "You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor the likeness of anything," and what follows. If, in saying "You shall not bow down to them" and "nor shall you serve them", he means these as two different things, then perhaps the following is the case. The one who is inwardly devoted to idols serves them. The one who is not so devoted, but out of cowardice, which he calls accommodation, makes a show of honoring them in order to seem as pious as the many, does not serve the idols but does bow down to them. And I would say that those who abjure Christianity, whether at the tribunal or before it, do not serve the idols but do bow down to them. They take the name of the Lord God, the name "God", in vain, applying it to vain and lifeless matter. In this way the people that was defiled with the daughters of Moab bowed down to idols but did not serve them. It is written in these very words: "They called them to the sacrifices of their idols, and the people ate of their sacrifices, and bowed down to their idols, and were initiated into Baal-Peor." Note that it does not say "and they served their idols." After so many signs and wonders, it was not possible for them to be persuaded in a single moment, by the women with whom they were committing fornication, to think that the idols were gods. Perhaps it was the same when the calf was made in Exodus: they bowed down to the calf they had watched being made, but did not serve it.

We must therefore consider the present trial a test and proving of our love for God. "For the Lord is testing you," as it is written in Deuteronomy, "to know whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul." But you, when you are tested, "will walk after the Lord your God, and fear him, and keep his commandments", especially "You shall have no other gods besides me", "and you will hear his voice and be joined to him". He takes you from these regions here and joins you to himself, into what the apostle called the growth of God in him.

Moreover, if "every evil word is an abomination to the Lord your God", how great an abomination must we consider the evil word of denial? And how great an abomination is the evil speech that proclaims another god, or the evil oath by the Fortune of men, a thing without real existence? When that oath is put to us, we must remember him who taught: "But I say to you, do not swear at all." Whoever swears by heaven offends against the throne of God. Whoever swears by earth commits impiety by deifying what is called the footstool of God's feet. Whoever swears by Jerusalem sins, even though it is the city of the great King, and whoever swears by his own head does wrong. How great a sin, then, must we consider swearing by someone's Fortune? At that moment we must also remember: "For every idle word you will give account on the day of judgment." For what word is as idle as an oath of denial?

The enemy will probably try by every means he can to trick us into worshiping the sun or the moon or all the host of heaven. But we shall say that the word of God did not command this. Created things must by no means be worshiped when the Creator is present, sufficient for all, and attentive to the prayers of all. Nor would the sun itself wish to be worshiped by those who belong to God's portion, and probably not by anyone else either. Rather, imitating him who said, "Why do you call me good? No one is good but one, God the Father," it would say, as it were, to anyone who wishes to worship it: "Why do you call me god? There is one true God. And why do you worship me? 'For you shall worship the Lord your God and serve him alone.' I too am created; why do you wish to worship one who himself worships? For I too worship and serve God the Father. Obeying his commands, I have been subjected to futility because of him who subjected me in hope. I too am now bound in a corruptible body, and I shall be set free from the bondage of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God."

We may also expect some prophet of impiety, perhaps not one but several. They will speak to us, as though it were a word of the Lord, what the Lord did not command, or, as though it were a word of wisdom, what is foreign to wisdom, so as to slay us with the word of their mouth. But even then, when the sinner stands against us, let us say: "But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and was like a mute who does not open his mouth; I became like a man who does not hear." For deafness to impious words is good when we despair of setting right those who speak what is evil.

In times when people summon us to the opposite course, it is useful for us to consider what God wishes to teach when he says, "I am the Lord your God, a jealous God." A bridegroom wants to turn his bride toward a chaste life. He wants her to gather her whole self toward him and to guard in every way against pouring herself out to anyone but him. If he is wise, he would display jealousy, using that display as a medicine for the bride. In the same way, I think, the one who speaks the oracle, especially if he is revealed to be "the firstborn of all creation", tells the bride, the soul, that he is a jealous God. In this way he draws his hearers away from all fornication with demons and with those who are reckoned to be gods. And as a God who is jealous in this way, he says of those who have in any way gone whoring after other gods: "They provoked me to jealousy with what is no god, they angered me with their idols; and I will provoke them to jealousy with what is no nation, with a foolish nation I will anger them. For a fire has been kindled by my wrath; it will burn to the depths of Hades."

A wise bridegroom, free from passion, may not turn his betrothed away from every defilement for his own sake. Yet for her sake, seeing her defilement and abomination, he will do everything that can heal her and turn her back. Since her nature is free, he offers her words that turn her away from fornication. What defilement could you think of worse for a soul than to proclaim some other god, whatever the manner, and not to confess the Lord who is truly one and only? And I think that just as "he who joins himself to a harlot is one body", so the one who confesses someone, especially in a time of torture and testing of faith, is blended and united with the one he confesses. But the one who denies is cut off by the denial itself, as if by a sword, from the one he denies. He suffers division and is separated from the one whom he denied. Consider, then, whether the following saying means that it follows necessarily for the one who confesses to be confessed, and for the one who denies to be denied: "Whoever confesses in me before men, I too will confess in him before my Father in heaven." The Word himself and the Truth himself might say both to the one who confessed and to the one who denied: "With the measure you measure, it will be measured back to you." "You who measured with the measure of confession toward me and filled up the measure of confession will receive from me a measure of confession, shaken together, pressed down, running over, which will be given into your bosom. And you who measured with the measure of denial and denied me will receive from me a measure of denial concerning you, in proportion to the measure of your denial."

We might consider in this way how the measure of confession is filled up, or else is not filled but falls short. Throughout the whole time of examination and trial, the devil wishes to defile us with evil thoughts of denial, of double-mindedness, or of some plausible argument that calls us toward what is hostile to martyrdom and perfection. We must give him no place in our hearts. Besides this, we must not defile ourselves with even a single word foreign to our confession. We must bear everything that comes from our adversaries: reproach, mockery, laughter and slander, and the pity with which they seem to pity us, supposing us deluded and foolish and calling us mistaken. Further, we must not be dragged and distracted toward possessions or toward this life by affection for our children, or for their mother, or for any of those reckoned dearest in this life. Instead, turning away from all these things, we must become wholly God's and belong wholly to the life with him and beside him, as those who are to share in his only-begotten Son and in those who partake of him. If we do all this, then we might say that we have filled up the measure of confession. But if we fall short in even one thing, we have not filled the measure of confession but defiled it, and have mixed something foreign into it. Therefore we shall need what is needed by those who have built wood, hay or straw upon the foundation.

We must also know this. We received what are called God's covenants on the terms of the compact we made with him when we undertook to live as Christians. Among the terms of our compact with God was the whole way of life according to the gospel, which says: "If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it, but whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it." Often we have been stirred more deeply on hearing this as well: "For what will a man profit if he gains the whole world but forfeits his soul? Or what will a man give in exchange for his soul? For the Son of Man is to come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each according to his deeds."

That one must deny oneself, take up one's own cross and follow Jesus was recorded not only by Matthew, whose words we have quoted, but also by Luke and Mark. Listen to Luke saying: "And he said to all: 'If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it, but whoever loses his soul for my sake will save it. For what does a man profit if he gains the whole world but loses or forfeits himself?'" And Mark: "And calling the crowd to him together with his disciples, he said to them: 'If anyone wishes to follow after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever wishes to save his own soul will lose it, but whoever loses it for the sake of the gospel will save it. For what will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul? For what will a man give in exchange for his soul?'"

Long ago, then, we ought to have denied ourselves and said, "It is no longer I who live." Now let it be shown whether we have taken up our cross and followed Jesus, which has happened if Christ lives in us. If we wish to save our soul so as to receive it back as something better than a soul, let us lose it by martyrdom. For if we lose it for Christ's sake, casting it upon him in death for his sake, we shall secure true salvation for it. But if we do the opposite, we shall hear that the one who has gained the whole visible world profits nothing, since he gained it at the cost of his own destruction, by forfeiting himself. Once someone has lost or forfeited his own soul, even if he gains the whole world, he will not be able to give it in exchange for the soul that is lost. For the soul, made in the image of God, is more precious than all bodies. Only one has been able to give an exchange for our soul, which had been lost before: he who bought us with his own precious blood.

For certain deeper reasons, too, Isaiah says: "I have given Egypt and Ethiopia and Syene as an exchange for you, because you have become precious in my sight." As for the precise account of this and of the rest: if, loving learning in Christ and wishing now at last to go beyond learning "through a mirror and in a riddle," you hasten to the one who called you, you will very soon know it "face to face," as friends of the Father and Teacher in heaven. For friends learn by sight and not through riddles. Rather, they learn by a wisdom stripped bare of sounds and words and symbols and types, and they reach the nature of intelligible things and the beauty of truth. If you believe that Paul was caught up to the third heaven, and caught up into paradise, and heard inexpressible words which a human being is not permitted to speak, it follows that you will know this: you will at once come to know more and greater things than the inexpressible words revealed to Paul then, after which he came down from the third heaven. And once you have this knowledge, you will not come down, if you take up the cross and follow Jesus, whom we have as a great high priest who has passed through the heavens. You yourselves, if you do not fall away from those who follow him, will pass through the heavens, going beyond not only the earth and the mysteries of the earth but also the heavens and what belongs to them. For far greater sights than these are stored up in God, sights that no nature in a body can take in unless it has first been set free from every body. For I am convinced that God reserves and keeps with himself far greater things than those which the sun and moon and the chorus of the stars have seen, and greater even than what the holy angels have seen, whom God made spirit and a flame of fire. He keeps them so that he may reveal them when the whole creation is set free from slavery to the enemy into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

So then, whoever among the [?] martyrs has something more than many martyrs, namely the love of learning in Christ, will ascend all the more quickly to what lies beyond. But you, holy Ambrose, if you examine the gospel saying carefully, can see that perhaps no one who has ever lived, or only very few, will obtain an exceptional and greater outpouring of blessedness. You too will be among them, if you swim through the contest without wavering. The words are these. Peter once said to the Savior: "Look, we have left everything and followed you. What then will there be for us?" And Jesus said to them (that is, to the apostles): "Truly I tell you, you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when God sits on the throne of his glory, you too will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel. And everyone who has left brothers or sisters or parents or children or fields or houses for the sake of my name will receive many times as much and will inherit eternal life." Because of these words, had I acquired as much on earth as you have, or even more, I would have prayed to become a martyr in Christ for God, so that I might receive many times as much, or, as Mark says, a hundredfold. And that is far more than the little we shall leave behind if we are called to martyrdom, once it is multiplied a hundred times.

For this reason, if I bear witness as a martyr, I would have wished to leave behind children as well, together with fields and houses. Then, with the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every family in heaven and on earth is named, I might be called the father of children many times more numerous and holier, or, to put it precisely, a hundred times more. And since there are fathers of whom it was said to Abraham, "But you shall go to your fathers in peace, nourished in a good old age," someone might say (I do not know whether truly): perhaps those fathers are men who once bore witness as martyrs and left their children, and in return for them have become fathers of the fathers of the patriarch Abraham and of other such patriarchs. For it is likely that those who left children behind and died as martyrs become fathers not of infants but of fathers.

Suppose someone, as if striving for the greater gifts, counts blessed the rich martyrs and the martyrs who are fathers, who will beget a hundredfold children and receive a hundredfold fields and houses. And suppose he asks whether it is reasonable for them to have a greater possession among intelligible things than martyrs who were poor in this life. We must tell him this. Those who endured tortures and pains displayed a more brilliant virtue in martyrdom than those who were not tested by these things. In the same way, there are those who cut through and broke so many worldly bonds, besides their love of the body and love of life. They showed great love toward God and truly took up the living word of God, which is active and sharper than any two-edged sword. Having cut through so many bonds and made wings for themselves like an eagle, they have been able to return to the house of their master. It is fitting, then, that those not tested by tortures and pains yield first place to those who showed their endurance on the rack, on various instruments of twisting, and in the fire. Just so, reason suggests that we who are poor, even if we die as martyrs, should yield first place to you. For the love of God in Christ, you trample on the deceptive glory that grips [?] the many, on such great possessions, and on affection for your children.

At the same time, notice the dignity of Scripture. It promises a multiplying, a hundredfold increase, of brothers and children and parents and fields and houses, but a wife is not counted among them. For it is not said: "Everyone who has left brothers or sisters or parents or children or fields or houses or wife for the sake of my name will receive many times as much." For in the resurrection of the dead they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels in heaven.

What Joshua said to the people when he settled them in the holy land, Scripture might now say to us as well. The passage runs: "Now fear the Lord and serve him in uprightness and in righteousness." And when we are being urged to worship idols, it will also say to us the words that follow: "Put away the foreign gods that your fathers served beyond the river and in Egypt, and serve the Lord."

At the beginning, when you were about to receive instruction in the faith, it might reasonably have been said to you: "But if it does not please you to serve the Lord, choose for yourselves today whom you will serve, whether the gods of your fathers beyond the river or the gods of the Amorites, among whom you dwell in the land." And your instructor would have said to you: "But I and my household will serve the Lord, for he is holy." Now, however, there is no room for these words to be said to you. For at that time you said: "Far be it from us to forsake the Lord in order to serve other gods. The Lord our God, he is God, who brought us and our fathers up out of Egypt and kept us safe all along the way by which we went." Moreover, in the covenants concerning godliness, you long ago gave your instructors this answer: "We too will serve the Lord, for he is our God." If, then, someone who breaks covenants made with human beings is an outlaw and a stranger to salvation, what must be said of those who, by denial, set aside the covenants they made with God and run back to Satan, whom they renounced when they were baptized? To such a person we must speak the words Eli spoke to his sons: "If a man sins against a man, they will pray for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who will pray for him?"

A great theater is gathering to watch you as you contend and are called to martyrdom. It is as if we said that this happens with athletes thought to be extraordinary, when countless thousands gather to watch their contest. And when you contend, you will say no less than Paul: "We have become a spectacle to the world, to angels and to human beings." So the whole world, and all the angels on the right and on the left, and all human beings, both those of God's portion and those of the others, will hear us as we fight the contest for Christianity. Either the angels in heaven will rejoice over us, and the rivers will clap their hands together, and the mountains will exult, and all the trees of the field will applaud with their branches; or (may it not happen) the powers below, which delight in evil, will rejoice. It is not out of place to see, from what is written in Isaiah, what those in Hades will say to those who have been conquered and have fallen away from heavenly martyrdom, so that we may shudder all the more at the impiety of denial. For I think words like these will be said to the one who has denied: "Hades below was embittered when it met you. All the giants who ruled the earth were roused up for you, those who raised all the kings of the nations from their thrones. All of them will answer and say to you..." And what will the conquered powers say to the conquered, those captured by the devil to those captured in denial? What are these words? "You too have been captured, as we were, and you have been counted among us." And if someone who had a great and glorious hope in God is defeated in the things of God through cowardice or through the pains inflicted on him, he will hear: "Your glory has gone down to Hades, your great gladness. Beneath you they will spread rottenness, and the worm will be your covering." And if someone often shone in the churches, appearing to them like the morning star, his good works shining before people, and afterward, while fighting the great contest, lost the crown of so great a throne, he will hear: "How the morning star that rose at dawn has fallen from heaven! He has been shattered on the earth." And this too will be said to him, since through denial he has become like the devil: "You will be cast out on the mountains like a loathsome corpse, with many dead who were pierced with swords and go down to Hades. As a garment soaked in blood will not be clean, so neither will you be clean." For how will anyone be clean who is defiled with blood and murder by the abominable fall of denial, and soaked in so great an evil?

Now let us show that we have heard the words "Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me." Let us take care that not even a doubt arises in us about whether we should deny or confess, so that the word of Elijah may not be spoken to us as well. It runs: "How long will you go limping on both your legs? If the Lord is God, follow him."

It is likely that we will also be reproached by our neighbors and mocked by some of those around us, who will shake their heads at us as at fools. But when these things happen, let us say to God: "You have made us a reproach to our neighbors, a mockery and a laughingstock to those around us. You have made us a byword among the nations, a shaking of the head among the peoples. All day long my disgrace is before me, and the shame of my face has covered me, at the voice of the one who reproaches and slanders, at the sight of the enemy and the persecutor." And when all these things happen, it is a blessed thing to say to God the words the prophet boldly adds after them: "All these things have come upon us, yet we have not forgotten you, and we have not dealt falsely with your covenant, and our heart has not turned back."

Let us remember that while we are in this life and consider the ways that lie outside this life, we say to God: "You have turned our paths aside from your way." Now is the time to recall that this region, in which we have been brought low, is a place of affliction for the soul, so that in our prayer we may say: "For you have brought us low in a place of affliction, and the shadow of death has covered us." And let us say this too with confidence: "If we have forgotten the name of our God, and if we have spread out our hands to a foreign god, will not God search this out?"

Let us strive to take up perfectly not only the open witness but also the hidden one, so that we too may declare, in the apostle's words: "For this is our boast, the testimony of our conscience, that we have conducted ourselves in the world in holiness and in the sincerity of God." And to the apostle's word let us join the prophet's: "For he knows the secrets of our heart." This holds above all if we are being led away to death. Then we will say to God what only martyrs say: "For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we are counted as sheep for the slaughter." And if ever the mind of the flesh suggests to us fear of the judges who threaten us with death, then let us say to them the words from Proverbs: "My son, honor the Lord, and you will be strong; but besides him fear no other."

The following too is useful for our present subject. Solomon says in Ecclesiastes: "I praised all the dead above the living, all who are alive until now." But which of the dead could be praised with such good reason as one who, by his own free choice, accepted death for the sake of godliness? Such was Eleazar. He chose death with glory rather than life with defilement, and of his own free choice went forward to the rack. He adopted a noble resolve, worthy of his ninety years, of the dignity of his old age, of the grey hair he had won with distinction, of his excellent upbringing from childhood, and still more of the holy legislation established by God. And he said: "It is not worthy of our age to pretend. Many of the young would suppose that Eleazar, at ninety, had gone over to a foreign way of life, and they too would be led astray through my pretense, for the sake of a short and fleeting life, and I would bring defilement and a stain upon my old age. For even if for the present I escape punishment from men, yet neither alive nor dead shall I escape the hands of the Almighty. Therefore, by bravely giving up my life now, I will show myself worthy of my old age, and I will leave the young a noble example of how to die a good death readily and nobly for the revered and holy laws."

I pray that when you come to the doors of death, or rather of freedom, you may say words like these, especially if pains are inflicted on you (for there is every reason to expect that you will suffer through the scheming of the opposing powers): "It is evident to the Lord, who has holy knowledge, that although I could have been set free from death, I endure harsh pains in my body as I am scourged, but in my soul I suffer these things gladly because of my fear of him." Such indeed was the death of Eleazar, so that it was said of him: "He left his death as an example of nobility and a memorial of virtue, not only to the young but to the great majority of the nation."

The seven brothers, too, recorded in the books of Maccabees, whom Antiochus tortured with whips and cords as they held fast to godliness, can be a most beautiful example of strong martyrdom for anyone who asks himself whether he is going to fall short of mere boys. Not only did each of them endure tortures himself, but after watching the torture of his brothers each also displayed a vigorous steadfastness in godliness. One of them, who became, as Scripture calls him, their spokesman, said to the tyrant: "What do you mean to ask and learn? For we are ready to die rather than transgress the laws of our fathers." And what need is there to tell what they endured from pans and cauldrons heated red-hot, so that they might be tortured in them after each had first suffered different things? The one named as their spokesman first had his tongue cut out. Then he was scalped, and he bore the scalping as others bear circumcision for the sake of the divine law, thinking that in this too he was fulfilling the word of God's covenant. And Antiochus, not content with this, cut off his hands and feet while the other brothers and their mother looked on at the sight. In this way he was punishing the brothers and the mother too, thinking he would shake their resolve with things that are considered so terrible. Still not content, when the earlier punishments had left the man's body useless, Antiochus ordered him to be brought, still breathing, to the fire under the pans and cauldrons and fried. As the vapor rose from the flesh of that most noble athlete of godliness, roasted by the tyrant's cruelty, the rest, with their mother, urged one another to die nobly. They comforted themselves with the thought that God was watching these things, for the conviction that the eye of God is present with those who endure was enough to give them endurance. And the president of the games for the athletes of godliness encouraged them. He was himself comforted and, if I may put it so, gladdened by those who rose above such great pains. It would be fitting for us too, when we find ourselves in such circumstances, to say to ourselves their words, which run like this: "The Lord God is watching, and in truth he is comforted over us."

When the first had been tested in this way, as gold is tested in a furnace, the second was led to the mockery. The servants of the tyrant's cruelty tore off his skin together with his hair and called on the sufferer to change his mind, asking whether he would eat of the things sacrificed to idols before his body was punished limb by limb. When he refused to change his mind, he was led to the next torture, and he kept his resolve to his last breath. In no way broken, nor yielding to the pains, he said to the impious king: "You accursed wretch, you release us from this present life, but the King of the world will raise us up, who have died for his laws, to an everlasting renewal of life."

The third, too, counted the pains as nothing and trampled on them out of love for God. When his tongue was demanded, he quickly put it out and boldly stretched out his hands, and said: "Since I give these up for the sake of God's laws, I hope to receive them back from God, such as God would give to the athletes of godliness toward him."

Likewise the fourth was tortured. He bore the torments and said: "It is better, when departing from among men, to wait for the hopes that come from God and to be raised by him in a resurrection to which the tyrant will not rise. For he will rise not to life but to reproach and everlasting shame."

Next he tortured the fifth. Looking at Antiochus, this brother reproached him with being mortal, since he did not curb his arrogance but thought that a tyranny lasting a few days was great power. And even in that state he declared that the nation had not been abandoned by God, who would very soon torment Antiochus and his offspring.

After him the sixth, as he was about to die, said: "Do not be deceived. We suffer these things willingly, paying the penalty for our own sins, so that we may be purified in our pains." And he told him that he must not think he would go unpunished for attempting to fight against God. For whoever fights against those who have been made divine by the Word is a fighter against God.

Last of all, Antiochus took the youngest in hand. He was convinced that this boy too was a brother of those who had counted such terrible pains as nothing, and that he shared their resolve. So he tried other approaches, thinking the boy could be won over by appeals and by sworn promises that he would make him rich and envied, if he gave up his ancestral customs, and would enroll him among his Friends and entrust him with royal offices. At first he achieved nothing, since the young man paid no attention to what was said, which he regarded as foreign to his own resolve. So Antiochus summoned the mother and urged her to advise the lad to save his life. She made a show of agreeing to persuade her son as the king wished. Then she mocked the tyrant and spoke many words to her son about endurance, so that the young man did not wait for the punishment that was coming. He went to meet it, calling on the executioners and saying: “Why are you waiting? Why do you delay? We obey the law given by God; we must not accept a command that opposes the divine words.” What is more, like a king passing sentence on those brought before him for trial, he passed judgment on the tyrant, judging him rather than being judged. He declared that, since the tyrant had raised his hands against the children of heaven, he would not escape the judgment of the almighty God who sees all things.

One could then see the mother of so many sons bearing bravely the sufferings and deaths of her sons, because of her hopes in God. For the dews of piety and the breath of holiness did not let the fire of a mother’s love be kindled in her heart, the fire that blazes up in many mothers as at the heaviest of misfortunes. I think it very useful for our present purpose to have set these things down here, abridged from the scripture. In this way we may see how much piety and love for God can do against the harshest pains and the heaviest tortures, since this love is far more powerful than any other love. Human weakness has no share in the life of this love for God. It is driven out of the whole soul as an exile and cannot act in the least, wherever there is someone able to say: “The Lord is my strength and my song,” and “I can do all things in Christ Jesus our Lord, who strengthens me.”

What martyrdom is, and how much boldness toward God it brings about, can also be learned from this. The saint, being generous and wishing to repay the benefits that have come to him from God, asks what he might do for the Lord in return for all he has received from him. He finds nothing else that a person of good will could render to God that would, as it were, balance his benefits, except death in martyrdom. For in the hundred and fifteenth psalm the question is written thus: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” And the reply to it, given by the one who asked what he should render to the Lord for all he had received from him, is stated thus: “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.” It is customary to call martyrdom “the cup of salvation,” as we have found in the Gospel. For when those who wanted to sit at Jesus’ right and left in his kingdom were reaching for greater honor, the Lord said to them: “Can you drink the cup that I drink?” By “cup” he meant martyrdom. This is also clear from the words: “Father, if it is possible, take this cup away from me; yet not what I will, but what you will.” Moreover, we learn that whoever drinks the cup that Jesus drank will sit with the King of kings, reign with him, and judge with him. This, then, is the cup of salvation: whoever takes it will call upon the name of the Lord, and everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved.

But someone who has not grasped the meaning of scripture may well suppose, because of the words “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” that the Savior himself, as it were, lost his nerve at the time of his passion. And if he lost his nerve, someone might say, who can ever be brave? First, we will ask those who suppose this about the Savior whether he was inferior to the one who says: “The Lord is my light and my savior; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers came near me to devour my flesh, my oppressors and my enemies, they grew weak and fell. If an army is drawn up against me, my heart will not fear. If war rises up against me, in this I will hope.” Perhaps these words spoken in the prophet belong to no one else but the Savior. Because of the light that came from the Father and the salvation that came from him, he feared no one; and because God defended him, he was afraid of nothing. His heart did not fear at all when the whole army of Satan was drawn up against him; and when war rose up against him, his heart, filled with God’s sacred teachings, hoped in God. So the same person cannot say out of cowardice, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” and also declare out of courage, “If an army is drawn up against me, my heart will not fear.”

So that nothing in this passage may escape us, notice the word “this” applied to the cup in all three Gospels. Matthew recorded the Lord as saying: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me”; Luke: “Father, if you are willing, take this cup away from me”; and Mark: “Abba, Father, all things are possible for you; take this cup away from me.” Every martyrdom is called a cup, whatever the manner of the death by which it is accomplished. Consider, then, whether you can say that when he said, “Let this cup pass from me,” he was not declining martyrdom as such (for then he would have said, “Let the cup pass from me”), but perhaps only this particular form of it. Consider also whether it is possible that the Savior was looking into the forms of cups, so to speak, and what would come about through each, and, grasping their differences with a most profound wisdom, declined this form of death in martyrdom and perhaps secretly asked for another, heavier one, so that some more universal benefit, reaching more people, might be accomplished through another cup. But it was not yet the Father’s will that this should happen, since he was arranging things by a way and an order wiser than the Son’s wish and than what the Savior saw. In the Psalms, clearly, the cup of salvation is the death of the martyrs. This is why “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” is followed by “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones.” Precious, then, is the death that comes to us, as God’s holy ones and not unworthy of him, if we die not the common death, so to speak, a death that does nothing for godliness, but an exceptional one: the death we die for Christianity, piety and holiness.

Let us also remember the sins we have committed. Let us remember that no one can receive forgiveness of sins without baptism; that according to the laws of the gospel no one can be baptized a second time with water and Spirit for the forgiveness of sins; and that the baptism of martyrdom is given to us. For that is what martyrdom is called, as is clear from the fact that “Can you drink the cup that I drink?” is followed by “or be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?” And elsewhere it is said: “I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!” Consider, too, whether the baptism of martyrdom, just as the Savior’s became a cleansing for the world, also serves to heal many who are cleansed by it. Those who served at the altar under the law of Moses were thought to minister forgiveness of sins to the people through the blood of goats and bulls. In the same way the souls of those beheaded for their testimony to Jesus do not serve at the altar in heaven in vain, but minister forgiveness of sins to those who pray. At the same time we also know that, just as the high priest Jesus Christ offered himself as a sacrifice, so the priests whose high priest he is offer themselves as a sacrifice; and because of this they are seen beside the altar as in their proper place. But among the priests, some were unblemished and offered unblemished sacrifices, and so served God, while others, marred by the blemishes Moses listed in Leviticus, were banished from the altar. And who is the unblemished priest offering an unblemished victim, if not the one who holds fast to his confession and fulfils every requirement that the principle of martyrdom demands? We spoke about this earlier.

We should not be surprised that the great blessedness of the martyrs, which will be spent in deep peace, calm and fair weather, must begin from a condition that seems rather gloomy and, so to speak, wintry. For first each of the blessed, traveling the narrow and hard road in winter, must show the seamanship he has acquired. Only then will come what is said in the Song of Songs to the bride who has swum through the winter: “My beloved answers,” it says, “and says to me: Arise, come, my companion, my fair one, my dove; for behold, the winter is past, the rain is over and gone.” And you too remember that you cannot hear “the winter is past” unless you struggle strongly and vigorously through the present winter. And after the winter has passed and the rain is over and gone, the flowers will appear; for those planted in the house of the Lord will flourish in the courts of our God.

We also know this: since we have been persuaded by Jesus to abandon idols and the godlessness of many gods, the enemy cannot persuade us to worship idols, but he wants to force us. That is why he does such things to those over whom he gains power, and he will make those he tempts either martyrs or idolaters. Even now he often says: “All these I will give you, if you fall down and worship me.” Let us take care, then, never to worship idols and subject ourselves to demons; for the idols of the nations are demons. What a thing it would be to abandon the kind yoke of Christ and his light burden, and to submit ourselves again to the yoke of demons and carry the burden of grievous sin! And this after we have come to know that the heart of idol-worshipers is ashes and their life more worthless than clay, and after we have said: “How false are the idols our fathers acquired, and there is none among them that sends rain.”

It was not only long ago that Nebuchadnezzar set up the golden image, nor only then that he threatened Hananiah, Azariah and Mishael that he would throw them into the fiery furnace if they did not worship it. Even now Nebuchadnezzar says the same things to us, who are true Hebrews, those who have crossed over. But so that we may experience the heavenly dew that quenches every fire from us and cools our minds, let us imitate those holy men. Perhaps even now Haman wants you, his Mordecais, to bow down to him; but you must say: “I will not set the glory of men above the glory of the God of Israel.” Let us overthrow Bel by the word of God and kill the dragon with Daniel, so that when we come near the mouths of lions we may suffer no harm from them, while only those who have brought this present contest upon us will be devoured by the lions that cannot swallow us. Let us hold fast to the fact that among Job’s brave deeds this is also mentioned: “If I put my hand to my mouth and kissed it, let this be counted against me as the greatest iniquity.” For it is likely that they will order us to put our hand to our mouth and kiss it.

Let us note this too: the Savior’s prophecies about martyrdom are found not in his discourses to the crowds but in those to the apostles. For after the words “These twelve Jesus sent out, instructing them: Do not go among the Gentiles,” and what follows, it continues: “Beware of men; for they will hand you over to councils and flog you in their synagogues, and you will be brought before governors and kings for my sake, as a testimony to them and to the Gentiles. When they hand you over, do not worry about how or what you are to speak; for what you are to speak will be given to you in that hour. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of the Father speaking in you. Brother will hand over brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise up against parents and have them put to death. And you will be hated by all because of my name. But whoever endures to the end will be saved. When they persecute you in this city, flee to the next; and if they persecute you there, flee to another. For truly I tell you, you will not finish going through the cities of Israel before the Son of Man comes.”

Luke records similar words: “When they bring you before the synagogues and the rulers and the authorities, do not worry about how you are to defend yourselves or what you are to say; for the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you ought to say.” And further on: “So make up your minds not to prepare your defense in advance; for I will give you a mouth and wisdom that none of your opponents will be able to withstand or contradict. You will be handed over even by parents and brothers, by relatives and friends, and they will put some of you to death; and you will be hated by all because of my name. But not a hair of your head will perish. By your endurance you will gain your souls.” Mark too says something similar: “When they lead you away and hand you over, do not worry beforehand or prepare what you are to say, but say whatever is given to you in that hour; for it is not you who speak, but the Holy Spirit. Brother will hand over brother to death, and a father his child, and children will rise up against parents and have them put to death. And you will be hated by all because of my name; but whoever endures to the end will be saved.”

These words, too, which in Matthew urge us to martyrdom, were spoken to no one but the Twelve. We too must listen to them, since by listening we shall become brothers of the apostles who heard them and shall be counted with the apostles. The words run as follows: “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul; rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.” And next the Lord teaches us that no one comes to the contest of martyrdom without providence. For it says: “Are not two sparrows sold for a penny? Yet not one of them will fall to the ground without your Father in heaven. And even the hairs of your head are all numbered. So do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows. Everyone, then, who confesses me before men, I too will confess before my Father in heaven; but whoever denies me before men, I too will deny before my Father in heaven.” The words in Luke have the same force: “I say to you, my friends, do not fear those who kill the body and after that can do nothing more. But I will show you whom to fear: fear him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna. Yes, I tell you, fear him. Are not five sparrows sold for two pennies? Yet not one of them is forgotten before God. Indeed, even the hairs of your head are all numbered. Do not be afraid; you are worth more than many sparrows. And I tell you, everyone who confesses me before men, the Son of Man also will confess before the angels of God; but whoever denies me before men will be denied before the angels of God.” And in another place: “For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his glory and that of the Father and of the holy angels.” Mark recorded something very similar to this: “For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of him the Son of Man also will be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”

Those who put us to death, then, kill the life of the body; for that is the meaning of “Do not fear those who kill the body,” said in these very words by both Matthew and Luke. And once they have killed the body, they cannot kill the soul, even if they want to; indeed, they “can do nothing more.” For how could a soul be destroyed that has been brought to life by its very confession? He who urges us to martyrdom in Isaiah bears witness to it in return, and so does his servant, where it is written: “Be my witnesses, and I too am a witness, says the Lord God, and so is the servant whom I have chosen.”

Observe this too: this command was given not to Jesus’ servants but to his friends: “Do not fear those who kill the body and after that can do nothing more.” We must fear, then, him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna. For he alone, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna. And he will indeed cast into it those who feared the ones who kill the body, and did not fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna, him who, after he has killed, has power to cast into Gehenna. If the hairs of anyone’s head are numbered, they are clearly numbered for those who are beheaded for Jesus’ sake. Let us confess in the Son of God before men, and not before gods, so that he who was confessed may repay us by confessing us before his God and Father, and he himself in heaven may confess the one who confessed him on earth.

Who, reckoning such things, will not exclaim with the apostle: “The sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us”? For how is confession before the Father not much greater than confession before men? How does the confession made in heaven by the one who has been confessed not surpass beyond all measure the confession on earth by which the martyrs confess the Son of God? And anyone who is thinking of denying him before men should remember the one who said, and cannot lie: “I too will deny him before my Father in heaven.”

Since Matthew recorded, “I too will confess him before my Father in heaven,” and Luke, “The Son of Man also will confess him before the angels of God,” I ask whether perhaps it is the firstborn of all creation, the image of the invisible God, who will confess before the Father in heaven the one who confessed him; while the one who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, and is therefore son of man, and who was born of a woman who was herself human and is therefore called Son of Man, by which is meant the man in Jesus, will confess before the angels of God those who confessed him. The corresponding account must be given of those who deny him.

We must also consider this: whoever confesses in the Son before men commends, as far as lies in him, Christianity and the Father of this Christianity to those before whom he confesses; while the one who is confessed by the firstborn of all creation and by the Son of Man is commended, through the confession of the Son of God and the Son of Man, to the Father in heaven and to the angels of God. Now, if it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends, how can we fail to regard as approved the one who has been judged worthy to be commended to the Father in heaven and to the angels of God? And if he is approved, and those like him, whom the Lord has tested like gold in the furnace through tortures and interrogations and accepted like a whole burnt offering, what must be said of those who were exposed in the furnace of temptation and denied him? He who denies those who deserve to be denied will deny them as unapproved before the Father in heaven and in the presence of the angels of God.

We must struggle not only against denying Christ, but also against being in the least ashamed of suffering what those estranged from God think shameful. This holds above all for you, holy Ambrose. Glorified and welcomed by a great many cities, you now march as if in a procession, carrying the cross of Jesus and following him as he leads you before governors and kings. He leads you so that, journeying with you, he himself may give you a mouth and wisdom. He gives them also to you, Protoctetus, his fellow contestant, and to those who bear witness with you both, you who are filling up what is lacking in the sufferings of Christ. And he leads you so that he may go with you into the paradise of God and show you how to pass through the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns and guards the way to the tree of life. Both of these guard the way to the tree of life, but they guard it so that no unworthy person may be allowed to pass through and reach the tree of life. The flaming sword will hold back those who have built wood, hay or straw on the foundation that has been laid, Jesus Christ. It will hold back above all the most combustible and longest-burning wood, which I may call the wood of denial. But the cherubim will receive those who by nature cannot be held by the flaming sword, because they have built nothing akin to it. The cherubim will escort them to the tree of life and to everything that God planted in the east and made spring up from the earth. With Jesus travelling with you to paradise, despise the serpent. He has been conquered and crushed under Jesus' feet, and through Jesus under yours as well, for Jesus has given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy, so that none of them can harm you.

So we must neither deny the Son of God nor be ashamed of him, or of those who belong to him, or of his words. We must listen to this: "Whoever denies me before others, I too will deny before my Father in heaven." We must also listen to this: "For whoever is ashamed of me and of mine, of that person the Son of Man will be ashamed when he comes in his glory and that of the Father and of the holy angels." And to this: "For whoever is ashamed of me and of my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, of that person the Son of Man will also be ashamed when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels."

Jesus too once endured a cross, despising the shame, and for this reason he sat down at the right hand of God. His imitators, who likewise despise shame, will sit with him and reign with him in the heavens. He came to cast peace not on the earth but on the souls of his disciples, and to cast a sword on the earth. The word of God is living and active, sharper than any two-edged sword, piercing to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and able to judge the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Because of this, now above all he makes the peace that surpasses all understanding, which he left to his apostles, rule in our souls. But he has cast a sword between the image of the earthly and the image of the heavenly. For the present he takes our heavenly part to himself, so that later, when we have become worthy not to be cut in two, he may make us wholly heavenly.

He came to cast on the earth not only a sword but also fire, of which he says: "How I wish it were already kindled!" So let this fire be kindled in you too, and let it consume every earthly thought of yours and every thought that loves the body. And the baptism with which Jesus was constrained until it was accomplished, receive it now with all eagerness. You who have a wife and children and brothers and sisters, remember this: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, he cannot be my disciple." And both of you remember this: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate, besides all these, his own life as well, he cannot be my disciple." But hate your own lives in such a way that by hating them you keep them for eternal life. For he says: "Whoever hates his life in this world will keep it for eternal life." So hate your life for the sake of eternal life, and be convinced that the hatred Jesus teaches us is good and beneficial. We must hate our life so that it may be kept for eternal life. In the same way, you who have a wife and children and brothers and sisters, hate them. Then you can benefit the very ones you hate, because by having hated them you will become a friend of God and gain the freedom to do them good.

At the same time, remember the one who prayed in the Spirit for the children of martyrs, left behind because of their parents' love for God, and said: "Preserve the children of those put to death." Only know that it is not the children of the flesh who are the children of God. To those descended from Abraham it is said: "I know that you are Abraham's offspring," and "If you were Abraham's children, you would do the works of Abraham." In the same way it will be said to your children: "I know that you are Ambrose's offspring," and "If you are Ambrose's children, do the works of Ambrose." And perhaps they will do them, since you will benefit them more after such a departure than if you had stayed with them. For then you will love them with greater knowledge and pray for them with greater understanding, if you learn that they are your children and not merely your offspring. Now keep these sayings on your lips: "Whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me," and "Whoever finds his life will lose it, and whoever loses his life for my sake will find it."

Through your eagerness for martyrdom, make room for the Spirit of your Father, who speaks to those handed over for the sake of godliness. If you see that you are hated and loathed and thought ungodly, then take up this saying: "This is why the world hates you, because you are not of this world. If you were of this world, the world would love its own." Since you came to believe you have endured many insults and many dangers for Christ's sake. Endure them to the end and grow in endurance, because "the one who endures to the end will be saved." Know that, as Peter says, you will rejoice, even though now for a little while, if it must be, you have been grieved by various trials. This is so that the genuineness of your faith, more precious than gold, which perishes even though it is tested by fire, may be found to result in praise and glory and honour at the revelation of Jesus Christ. But take "grieved" to mean "having toiled". This is clear also from "In grief you shall bear children", for a woman does not necessarily give birth in grief as an emotion, but she does give birth in toil.

This saying is useful for the disciples of Christ: "Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For everything in the world, the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes and the pride of life, is not from the Father but is from the world. And the world is passing away, and its desire too." So do not love what is passing away. Instead, do the will of God and become worthy to be made one with the Son and the Father and the Holy Spirit, as the Saviour prayed when he said: "As I and you are one, so that they too may be one in us." How many days can a person gain by loving the world or the things in the world? Meanwhile he forfeits or loses his own soul, and he carries around a conscience heavier than a heavy burden, weighed down by the fall of denial. Let each of us recall how often he has been in danger of dying the common death. And let us consider whether we were preserved for this very purpose: to be baptized in our own blood, to wash away every sin, and to spend our days beside the altar in heaven with those who have contended alongside us.

Someone might give way, out of great love of life, or softness in the face of pain, or the arguments that seem persuasive when people try to lure us towards what is worse. If such a person denies that there is one God and his Christ, and confesses demons or the Fortunes, let him know this. He is preparing a table for the demon and filling a mixing bowl for Fortune. He has forsaken the Lord and forgotten his holy mountain, and he will face the reproofs that Isaiah wrote down as follows: "But you who have forsaken me and forgotten my holy mountain, who prepare a table for the demon and fill a mixing bowl for Fortune, I will hand you over to the sword, and you shall all fall in the slaughter. For I called you and you did not obey; I spoke and you did not listen. You did what was evil in my sight and chose what I did not want. Therefore thus says the Lord, the Lord: See, my servants shall eat, but you shall go hungry. See, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty. See, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame. See, my servants shall exult with gladness, but you shall cry out for anguish of heart and wail for a broken spirit. For you shall leave my name to my chosen ones for their fill, but the Lord will destroy you." If we understand what the Lord's table is and want to share in it, let us remember this: "You cannot share in the table of the Lord and the table of demons." And consider the saying "From now on I will not drink of this fruit of the vine until that day when I drink it new in the kingdom of heaven." If we understand what it means and want to be found among those who drink with Jesus, let us heed this: "You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons."

John, the son of thunder, says: "He who denies the Father and the Son... Everyone who denies the Son does not have the Father either. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also." Who that hears these words will not fear to deny the Son by saying that he is not a Christian, since by denying him he will not have the Father? And who would not be moved to confess by deeds and words that he is a Christian, so that he too may have the Father? For those who confess have the Father.

We have passed from death to life by passing from unbelief to faith. If so, let us not be surprised if the world hates us. No one who has not passed from death to life but remains in death can love those who have passed from the dark house of death, if I may call it that, into the buildings made of living stones and filled with the light of life. Jesus laid down his life for us. So let us also lay down ours, I will not say for him, but for ourselves, and I think also for those who will be built up by our martyrdom. The time has come for us Christians to boast. For Paul says: "And not only that, but we also boast in our afflictions, knowing that affliction produces endurance, and endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope. And hope does not put us to shame", provided only that the love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit. Let Paul say: "If, humanly speaking, I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus"; but let us say: "If, humanly speaking, I was put to death in Germany."

Just as the sufferings of Christ abound, so through Christ comfort also abounds. If so, let us most eagerly welcome the sufferings of Christ, and let them abound in us, if we long for abundant comfort. All who mourn will be comforted with this comfort, though perhaps not equally. For if the comfort were equal, it would not have been written: "Just as the sufferings of Christ abound for us, so our comfort also abounds." Those who share in the sufferings will also share in the comfort, in proportion to the sufferings they share with Christ. You learn this too from the one who speaks of such things with assurance: "For we know that as you share in the sufferings, so you share also in the comfort."

God says through the prophet: "At an acceptable time I heard you, and on a day of salvation I helped you." What time, then, could be more acceptable than when, for the sake of our devotion to God in Christ, we are led away under guard? We march in procession through the world, celebrating a triumph rather than being led in one. For the martyrs in Christ, together with him, strip the principalities and powers and triumph with him. They have become sharers in his sufferings, and so also in the mighty deeds done in his sufferings. Among these deeds is his triumph over the principalities and powers, which in a little while you will see conquered and put to shame. What other day is so truly a day of salvation as the day of our departure from here in this way? But I urge you: give no offence in anything, so that the presbyterate or the diaconate may not be blamed because of you. Rather, in everything commend yourselves as ministers of God. Commend yourselves in great endurance, saying: "And now what is my endurance? Is it not the Lord?" Commend yourselves in afflictions, convinced that many are the afflictions of the righteous. Commend yourselves in hardships, so that we may claim blessedness as our necessary due. Commend yourselves in distresses, so that we may travel the narrow and hard way without turning aside and arrive at life. If need be, let us commend ourselves also in beatings, in prisons, in riots, in labours, in sleepless nights and in fasting. For behold, the Lord comes, and his reward is in his hand, to repay each according to his works.

Now let us show that we longed for knowledge because of the works that befit knowledge. Let every kind of purity, free from every defilement of any sin whatever, be made manifest in us. As sons of a long-suffering God and brothers of a long-suffering Christ, let us be long-suffering in everything that befalls us; for "a long-suffering man is great in understanding, but the faint-hearted is utterly foolish." If one must commend oneself "by the weapons of righteousness for the right hand and for the left," then, having commended ourselves through glory without being puffed up by it, let us now also endure dishonor. If we have lived in a way worthy of good report and have been well spoken of, let us now also bear the ill report that comes from the ungodly. Further, if lovers of truth have admired us as truthful, let us now laugh when we are said to be deceivers. In the many dangers from which we have been rescued, many said that we were known by God; now let anyone who wishes say that we are unknown, at a time when perhaps we are known all the more. So, bearing what befalls us, we are chastened but not put to death, and we who rejoice look like those who sorrow.

Somewhere Paul speaks to those who had endured at the beginning, urging them, in keeping with their earlier endurance, to bear a second round of dangers for the sake of the word: "Remember the former days, in which, after you were enlightened, you endured a great contest of sufferings, sometimes being made a public spectacle through reproaches and afflictions, and sometimes becoming partners with those who were so treated. For you sympathized with me in my chains, and you accepted the plundering of your possessions with joy, knowing that you have a better possession, and an abiding one. Do not, then, throw away your confidence, which has a great reward. For you have need of endurance." Let us, therefore, now also endure a great contest of sufferings, being made a public spectacle through reproaches and afflictions, and accepting with joy the plundering of our possessions; for we are persuaded that we have a better possession, not earthly, nor even bodily, but invisible and incorporeal. For we look not to the things that are seen, perceiving that these are temporary, while those are eternal.

But since some, failing to consider the doctrine about demons—that in order to remain in this thick air around the earth they need the nourishment that comes from exhalations, and so they keep watch wherever there is always the smoke of sacrifice, and blood, and incense—make light of sacrificing as a matter of indifference, we would say to this too: if those who supply food to robbers, murderers, and barbarian enemies of the great king are punished as having wronged the commonwealth, how much more justly would those be accused who, by sacrificing, give food to the servants of wickedness that keeps them confined to the region around the earth—especially if, after learning the words "He who sacrifices to other gods, and not to the Lord alone, shall be utterly destroyed," they should sacrifice to the authors of the evils on earth. And indeed I think that, for the sins committed by the demons as they work against human beings, those who fed them by sacrificing will be accused no less than the demons who carried out the evil deeds. For it is as though the demons and those who kept them on earth had done these evils to humanity jointly, since the demons could not have survived without the exhalations and the foods that are thought to be suited to their bodies.

Again, some suppose that names are a matter of convention and have no natural connection with the things of which they are the names, and so they think it makes no difference whether one says, "I worship the first God," or "Dia," or "Zen," or whether one declares, "I honor and acknowledge the sun," or "Apollo," and "the moon," or "Artemis," and "the spirit in the earth," or "Demeter," and all the other things the wise men of the Greeks speak of. To these it must be said that there is a very deep and recondite study concerning names, and whoever understands it will see that, if names were a matter of convention, the so-called demons or any other powers invisible to us would not obey those who know the names but pronounce them as if they had been conventionally assigned. As it is, certain sounds and syllables, and names uttered with rough or smooth breathing, or with long or short vowels, perhaps draw those who are called by some nature hidden from our view. If this is so, and names are not a matter of convention, then the first God must be called by no name other than those by which his servant, the prophets, and our Savior and Lord himself name him—such as Sabaoth, Adonai, Shaddai, and again, "the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob"; for this, he says, "is my eternal name and my memorial to generations of generations." It is no wonder that the demons apply their own names to the first God, in order to be worshiped as the first God. But this was not the ancestral custom of our servant, of the prophets, of Christ, the fulfillment of the law, or of his apostles. I have set these things down of necessity, so that no one may outwit us with sophistry or, even to some small degree, defile our reasoning. We must pay careful heed to them, giving no opening for the attacks of our adversaries.

And yet a man still clings to life, even when he has become persuaded about the nature of the rational soul as having something akin to God. For both are intellectual and invisible and, as the prevailing argument demonstrates, incorporeal. Why would the one who fashioned us have implanted in us a longing for piety toward himself and for fellowship with him—a longing that, even in those who have gone astray, preserves some traces of the divine will—if it were not possible and attainable for rational beings to grasp what they naturally long for? It is clear that, just as each of our members is naturally suited to some corresponding object—the eyes to visible things and the ears to audible things—so the mind is suited to intelligible things and to God, who is beyond intelligible things. Why, then, do we shrink back and hesitate to put off the corruptible body that hinders us, that weighs down the soul, the earthly tent that burdens the much-thinking mind, to be set free from our bonds and to depart from the waves that come with flesh and blood? So that, with Christ Jesus, we may enjoy the rest that belongs to blessedness, contemplating him, the Word, who is wholly and entirely living, being nourished by him, grasping the manifold wisdom that is in him, being formed by Truth itself, and having our mind illuminated by the true and unceasing light of knowledge, so that we behold the things that by nature are seen through that light, with eyes enlightened by the commandment of the Lord.

Long ago we heard the words of Jesus, and for a long time now we have been disciples of the gospel, and all of us have built ourselves a house. But where we built it—whether on the rock, after digging and going deep, or on the sand without a foundation—the present contest will show. For a storm has come upon us, bringing rain and rivers and winds, or, as Luke calls it, a flood; and when these beat against the house, either they will not be able to shake it, and so the house will not fall, since it is founded on the rock, which is Christ; or they will expose the unsoundness of the building, which will collapse on the present occasion. May this be far from our buildings! For very great is the fall that comes with denial, or, as Luke says, great is the ruin of the building that has no foundation. Let us therefore pray that we may be like the wise man who built his house on the rock. Then let it come against such a building—the rain from the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, or the rivers of the principalities and powers that are our enemies, or the harsh winds from the world rulers of this darkness, or the flood of the spirits under the earth—and let them dash themselves against our building on the rock; so that the house not only does not fall but is not even shaken at all, and the powers at work suffer at our hands rather than accomplish anything. And let each of you say, as he strikes his adversaries: "So I box, not as one beating the air."

Moreover, since the sower has gone out to sow, let us show that our soul has received his seed—not like those along the path, nor like the rocky ground, nor like the thorns, but like the good soil.
